paper_title: DIY-MKG An LLM-Based Polyglot Language Learning System
caption: DIY-MKG reliably expands the vocabulary with low sensitivity to the language and the starting word. For each language, 10 opaque curves represent vocabulary sizes obtained from 10 different starting words, and one solid curve represents the average of the 10 curves. The standard deviations across languages and starting words are small, indicating fairness for all language learners. The diagonal gray line represents the upper-bound of vocabulary size, assuming all words in each iteration have not yet appeared in the vocabulary. While the real expansion rate is lower, the vocabulary does not saturate after 500 iterations. Therefore, DIY-MKG can reliably help the language learner to expand their vocabulary by consistently introducing new words.
model_annotation: The plot illustrates the growth of vocabulary size over 500 iterations for three languages—Spanish (blue), Korean (orange), and Japanese (green)—within the DIY-MKG system. The x-axis, labeled “Number of Iterations,” spans from 0 to 500 with linear scaling and tick marks at intervals of 100. The y-axis, labeled “Vocabulary Size,” ranges from 0 to 5000, also on a linear scale, with tick marks every 1000 units. For each language, a solid line represents the average vocabulary size across 10 different starting words, while 10 semi-transparent, overlapping curves of the same color show individual runs, indicating low variance. All three solid lines begin near (0, 0) and rise steadily: Spanish reaches approximately 3,000 at 500 iterations, Korean slightly below that, and Japanese slightly above. A gray diagonal line, representing the theoretical upper bound where every new word is unique, rises linearly from (0, 0) to (500, 5000). The actual vocabulary growth for all languages remains well below this bound but continues to increase without plateauing, suggesting no saturation. The tight clustering of the opaque curves around each solid line confirms low sensitivity to starting word and consistent performance across languages.
